content.title: Where Grammarly attaches to the writing
content.body: Grammarly is designed to help people revise text in the places they already write, depending on the supported app, browser, or editor integration. The practical benefit is less context switching while drafting emails, documents, and other everyday text. Before adopting it for a team, test the exact applications and document types employees use, and confirm whether the relevant integration is supported on their devices and plan.

content.title: What Grammarly checks in a paragraph
content.body: Use Grammarly to review a representative paragraph for spelling, grammar, punctuation, clarity, tone, and other suggestions available in the current product. Recommendations are not automatically correct: proper names, technical language, quotations, and deliberate stylistic choices may need to be retained. Compare the original and revised text, and define when human review is required for customer-facing, legal, medical, or otherwise high-impact writing.
items: Tone detection across sentences and whole drafts
Clarity rewrites that cut wordiness from a paragraph
Engagement suggestions for flat or generic phrasing
Fluency rephrases and plagiarism checking on paid tiers

content.title: Style guides and brand tones for teams
content.body: For teams, shared style guidance can help writers use consistent terminology and voice, but the available team controls depend on the current subscription and product configuration. Start with a short style guide, a list of preferred terms, and a real document. Check how the tool handles exceptions, specialized vocabulary, and different audiences before rolling out shared rules.

content.title: What Grammarly will not do
content.body: Grammarly can support editing and may offer additional AI-assisted writing capabilities, but it should not be treated as a substitute for subject-matter review, fact checking, or editorial ownership. It can suggest fluent wording that changes meaning or introduces unsupported detail. Use it to assist revision, then verify factual claims, sources, tone, and audience fit yourself.

content.title: Two pricing files that disagree
content.body: This review's own fields record Grammarly as freemium with a band of $12-30/mo. Two files in this repository quote entry pricing differently: one records roughly $12 per month for a paid individual plan, another records a higher per-user band for business plans. Because those entries conflict, treat the band as indicative and confirm current pricing with the vendor before budgeting. No figure beyond the band held on this page comes from anywhere else, and nothing on this page is drawn from a use of the product.

content.title: Deployment and what is not on file
content.body: Grammarly is recorded as a hosted product whose API field is marked available, and delivery runs through the browser extension, Office add-in, and desktop app, so text passes through the vendor's service while being checked. No compliance certification appears anywhere in the material assembled for Grammarly, and no such assertion appears here. For a tool that reads correspondence, drafts, and internal documents, the questions worth pressing with the vendor are about data retention on checked text, whether customer content trains shared models, and how deletion is honored across regions.

content.title: Grammarly against the generators
content.body: Eleven pages of comparisons in this repository pair Grammarly with other products. Its traditional antagonists are the chat assistants and generators — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Jasper, Copy.ai, Writesonic — where the trade is breadth of generation against precision of correction. Pairings with creative tools such as Midjourney, Runway, and Synthesia show up mainly as category contrast: they produce images, video, and avatar scripts, while Grammarly only edits text. For a buyer the distinction is simple — if the problem is finished prose drifting off-tone or off-grammar, Grammarly is the narrower and more appropriate instrument.

content.title: Who should install Grammarly, and who should not
content.body: Grammarly is worth evaluating when the main need is to improve text that already exists, especially across everyday writing tools. It may be less useful for teams that rarely produce prose, need guaranteed factual accuracy, or cannot send the relevant text to a third-party service under their data policies. Test it with real but non-sensitive examples, review false positives, and decide which types of documents require a human editor regardless of tool suggestions.

faqs.question: Is Grammarly a generator or an editor?
faqs.answer: Grammarly is primarily useful for revising existing text: checking spelling, grammar, punctuation, clarity, and tone in supported writing environments. Test it with the document types and applications your team actually uses.

faqs.question: Which languages does Grammarly support best?
faqs.answer: Language support and the quality of suggestions can vary by language, feature, and application. Check Grammarly's current language documentation, then test representative writing samples—including technical terms and proper names—before relying on it for a team's workflow.

faqs.question: What do I get with Grammarly Business?
faqs.answer: Team features and administration controls depend on the current plan. Verify available style guidance, user management, privacy controls, supported apps, AI usage, and billing terms in the official documentation before purchasing.

faqs.question: How much does Grammarly cost?
faqs.answer: Current Grammarly prices and plan terms are not independently verified here. Check the official pricing page for current billing, supported features, AI usage limits, team controls, and renewal terms, then estimate cost for your actual user count.

faqs.question: Can Grammarly work inside Microsoft Word and email?
faqs.answer: Grammarly works with selected editors and applications through supported integrations, but availability can change by platform and account type. Check the current compatibility list and test the exact Microsoft Word or email workflow your team uses.

learningCurve: Very low — once installed in the browser it runs unattended and corrections appear as text is typed
whoShouldUse: Individual writers and teams whose day is mostly written communication, and organizations that want style guides and brand tones enforced at the keyboard instead of during a late editorial pass.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams that need documents generated from a prompt, researchers managing long-form arguments and citations, or buyers who need a documented compliance record before rollout.
